h1: Writing about beer for a living
title: Writing About Beer for a Living | Craft Beer School
desc: What paid beer writing really looks like in India: the kinds of work, the skills editors want and how to build a portfolio without losing your integrity.
teaser: Very few people are paid only to write about beer. Plenty are paid to write about it some of the time.
standfirst: Beer writing sounds like the dream job. In practice it is a patchwork of freelance pieces, brand work and tasting notes, held together by knowing the subject properly and writing clearly.
sections:
Full-time beer writer jobs are rare everywhere. India is no exception. Most people who earn from writing about beer do several things at once: freelance articles for food and travel outlets, content for breweries, tasting notes for menus, copywriting, judging and sometimes teaching.

That mix is not a failure. It is how the work is built. The writers who last treat beer as a speciality inside a broader writing practice instead of the only thing they will ever cover.

• Editorial: features, reviews and city guides for food, drink and travel publications.
  • Brewery content: website copy, beer descriptions, newsletters and social posts.
  • Menus and tasting notes: short, precise descriptions that help a bar sell beer.
  • Trade writing: articles for people inside the industry, which pay for technical accuracy.
  • Books and longer projects: slow and uncertain, but they build a reputation.

Brand work in India comes with a constraint. Alcohol advertising is heavily restricted, so breweries are careful about what they publish and where. Our guide to alcohol advertising rules in India explains why a brief may look oddly cautious.
Knowing the subject is the job

Editors can find people who write well. What they struggle to find is someone who writes well and gets the beer right. A writer who calls every hazy beer "unfiltered" or describes diacetyl as "a lovely buttery note" in a pilsner loses credibility with every brewer who reads it.

Learn how to taste beer methodically and learn the major styles. Then learn how beer is made. Knowing that butterscotch in a lager usually means the fermentation was cut short lets you write something a brewer respects and a reader learns from. This is where many keen writers hit a wall: they have the vocabulary of enthusiasm but not the vocabulary of process.

Start by publishing your own work somewhere you control, such as a blog or a newsletter. Write about specific beers, breweries and ideas instead of vague praise for craft beer in general. Visit breweries and ask the brewers real questions. Their answers make better stories than your opinions alone.

Then pitch. A good pitch to an editor is short: the story, why now, why you. Indian food and drink publications and regional newspapers are more realistic first targets than international magazines.

Be patient with rejections and with silence, which is the more common reply. Keep a list of what you pitched, to whom and when. Follow up once after a couple of weeks, then move on. Over time the editors who liked your work will start coming to you with ideas.

Breweries will send you beer and invite you to launches. That is normal. Say so when a beer was given to you or a trip was paid for. Do not let it soften a review. Readers trust writers who are visibly honest. Breweries respect them more in the end.

Write responsibly too. Celebrate flavour and craft, not quantity. Never write anything that glamorises drinking and driving or targets readers under the legal age.
What a good tasting note looks like

Short commercial writing is where most beer writers start earning, so it is worth learning to do it well. A good tasting note for a menu tells the drinker what they will actually taste, in words they understand, in under forty words. It names the style, the main aromas, the body and the finish. It avoids "crisp and refreshing", which describes almost every beer ever sold in India.

Compare two versions. "A refreshing craft beer bursting with flavour" tells the reader nothing. "A pale, dry wheat beer with banana and clove from the yeast, light body and a soft finish" tells them whether to order it. The second one needs the writer to know what a hefeweizen yeast does.

Practise by writing notes for every beer you drink and comparing them with the brewery's own description. You will quickly find where your vocabulary is thin.

Many beer writers add a tasting qualification or judging experience, which deepens their palate and their credibility. See our guides to a beer sommelier career and judging. Others move into brewery marketing or education. The common thread is the same: know the beer, explain it plainly.
faqs: Can I make a full-time living writing about beer in India?
It is possible but uncommon. Most people combine beer writing with other writing, brand work, judging or teaching.
Do I need a brewing qualification to write about beer?
No, but real knowledge of tasting and brewing makes your writing far more credible to editors, brewers and readers.
Is it ethical to accept free beer as a writer?
It is common and acceptable if you disclose it clearly and keep your judgement independent.
